mcqs.question: What's the primary architectural difference between the multi-cluster shared-data, serverless, and fixed-cluster MPP compute models?
options: How compute is provisioned, scaled, and billed — not the underlying MPP and columnar query execution principles
Only fixed-cluster platforms use columnar storage at all
Serverless platforms cannot run analytical aggregation queries
Multi-cluster platforms don't support SQL
mcqs.explanation: All three models implement the same underlying MPP and columnar principles; they differ in how compute capacity is provisioned, scaled, and charged for. Columnar storage isn't exclusive to fixed-cluster platforms, serverless platforms are built specifically for analytical aggregation, and SQL support is universal across all three models.

mcqs.question: In a multi-cluster shared-data model, why can a data science team's heavy nightly job run without affecting the BI team's dashboard queries during the day?
options: The two teams are using entirely separate copies of the underlying data
Only one team's cluster is allowed to run at any given time
Each team's cluster is independently sized, scaled, and billed while reading the same shared underlying data, so neither competes for the other's compute resources
Dashboard queries are automatically prioritized over batch jobs on the same cluster
mcqs.explanation: Because compute clusters are independent even though they share one copy of the underlying data, one team's heavy workload on its own cluster simply doesn't consume the other team's cluster's resources. The data isn't duplicated, both clusters can run concurrently, and there's no need for query prioritization since they're physically separate compute resources.

mcqs.question: Under a serverless warehouse's consumption-based pricing, what has the most direct effect on cost per query?
options: How many total tables exist in the warehouse
How much data the query actually scans, since billing tracks bytes processed rather than cluster uptime
What time of day the query runs
How many columns the destination table has, regardless of which columns the query selects
mcqs.explanation: Serverless billing tied to bytes processed means the amount of data a specific query actually scans directly drives its cost — which is exactly why column pruning and predicate pushdown discipline matter more under this model. Total table count, time of day, and unselected columns in a wide table don't directly affect a query's own bytes-processed cost.

mcqs.question: For which kind of workload does a fixed-cluster model tend to be most cost-efficient compared to elastic alternatives?
options: A workload with frequent, unpredictable concurrency spikes
A workload that runs only once a month for a few minutes
A workload split across many teams with wildly different usage patterns
A steady, well-understood workload with predictable volume and shape
mcqs.explanation: A fixed-cluster's cost advantage comes from being sized once for a workload that doesn't need elastic scaling — predictable, steady usage avoids paying for the elasticity overhead that unpredictable or bursty workloads actually need. Unpredictable spikes, rare bursts, and highly varied multi-team usage are exactly the cases elastic models handle better.

mcqs.question: A fixed-size cluster is handling one large query fine, but chokes when a hundred modest queries arrive simultaneously. What does this illustrate?
options: Query size and query concurrency are separate axes, and a platform's single-large-query performance doesn't predict its behavior under concurrent bursts
The cluster's query engine is fundamentally broken
This proves fixed clusters can never handle more than one query at a time
Concurrency issues only occur with serverless platforms, never fixed clusters
mcqs.explanation: This is exactly the distinction the slide draws — a platform can handle a large query well while still hitting a hard concurrency ceiling once many queries arrive at once, since those are different capacity dimensions. It's not evidence of a broken engine, fixed clusters do handle more than one concurrent query up to their capacity, and concurrency ceilings are a fixed-cluster characteristic specifically, not a serverless-only issue.

mcqs.question: A team migrates from a fixed-cluster platform to a serverless one, porting their wide table and SELECT * queries unchanged. Why might their bill increase even though usage patterns didn't change?
options: Serverless platforms always charge more than fixed-cluster platforms for identical workloads

Under fixed-cluster pricing, cost was tied to cluster-hours regardless of bytes scanned; under serverless, cost tracks bytes actually processed, so the same broad-scan queries now cost proportionally more
SELECT * queries are technically incompatible with serverless platforms
Migrating platforms always requires re-writing all existing data from scratch
mcqs.explanation: The cost mechanism changed from cluster-hours to bytes-processed, so query patterns that were cost-neutral under the old model directly inflate cost under the new one — the pricing model, not usage, is what shifted. Serverless isn't inherently more expensive across the board, SELECT * runs fine on serverless platforms technically, and a migration doesn't require rewriting existing data by default.
